articles.title: Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.
Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200 , has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post . It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March .

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg .

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.
Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.
“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.
The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.
“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.
“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

articles.title: No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat , which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.
Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.
“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”
“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.
The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.
Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.
When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.
“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.
Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit , a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.
Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.
Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.
The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.
Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.
Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.
The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.
“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners .

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.
Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB) , her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.
Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”
Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.
The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.
“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.
Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together . So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.
Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.
Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.
“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.
“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”
Editor’s note: Mary Brunkow is speaking Nov. 13 from 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at EY in Seattle as part of Technology Alliance’s Discovery Series . Register here .

articles.title: Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.
Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.
A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.
Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.
“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC , which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”
Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.
“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

articles.title: Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members . Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.
Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

articles.title: Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”
Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”
It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.
For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.
The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

articles.title: Seattle Police Department Enjoys Unique Privileges, Insulation from Accountability
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Seattle’s public safety departments – particularly the Seattle Police Department (SPD) – have historically received unique treatment and favored allocation of resources, including both money and technological tools. Reviewing recent developments in the City of Seattle, that special treatment does not look to disappear any time soon.

Until it was terminated after 15 years by Judge James Robart last fall, SPD’s consent decree acted as a reminder of the impunity under which SPD had routinely been allowed to operate. The dismissal of the consent decree was postponed after SPD officers responded to the George Floyd protests of 2020 with violence and the indiscriminate use of less lethal weapons such as tear gas, pepper spray, and rubber bullets.

In the final consent decree hearing , Robart repeatedly talked about how the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG) contract had “neutered” Seattle’s police accountability ordinance. While utilization of the Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) team has recently improved following the departure of former SPD Chief Shon Barnes, the SPOG contract has also hampered the CARE team’s ability to respond to appropriate calls.

SPD receives a large share of the City’s discretionary General Fund. Public safety as a whole accounts for 53% of the $2 billion of General Fund expenditures in Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed 2027 budget, and by itself, SPD receives more than a quarter of the total General Fund.

That largesse comes in spite of the lack of fiscal responsibility demonstrated by the department. One recent example: in June of this year, SPD overpaid about 900 of their employees by $13.1 million due to a “payroll error.” Because most of these employees are represented by SPOG, the City will have to negotiate with SPOG to try to recover the bulk of these funds, meaning it could be years before the money returns to the City’s coffers.

Four and a half months after the error, neither the Mayor’s Office nor SPD would comment about whether they have identified the person or persons responsible for this mistake or whether any disciplinary action would be taken.

In addition, neither the Mayor’s Office nor SPD shared any plans to avoid such errors in the future. While the overpayment was one time in nature since it was caused by an error in the calculation of payment of retroactive pay increases provided by recent union contracts, it could presumably be made again the next time new contracts require a similar calculation.

SPD receives special budgetary consideration beyond the mere size of its annual budget in the way the department routinely overspends its overtime budget. Data from a council central staff report in 2015 showed that SPD had overspent its overtime all but one year from 1995-2014, a trend that has continued, including this year and last year .

SPD has also traditionally received an extra slush fund through “ghost cop” positions , funded officer positions that will definitely not be filled. While these positions have finally been eliminated, under the current 2027 budget proposal, SPD is expected to achieve $4.5 million in salary savings.

The Seattle Fire Department (SFD) might also get in on the slush fund act. SFD took a cut to its overtime budget in Wilson’s proposed 2027-2028 budget, with two competing budget amendments from councilmembers looking to address this cut. Budget Chair Dan Strauss and Councilmember Maritza Rivera had identical amendments proposing to restore SFD’s overtime by the full $7.1 million amount of the cut.

Councilmember Dionne Foster’s amendment, on the other hand, suggested increasing SFD’s overtime by $5.1 million. Foster had asked council’s central staff to do an analysis to come up with this number based on the number of new hires at SFD, as well as the likelihood that some shifts at SFD would remain uncovered due to lack of volunteers to do overtime. Foster’s goal was to achieve the same target daily staffing level with fewer dollars.

“If SFD does receive this $7.1 million in overtime funding, but does not spend it all for that purpose, that funding will be in the SFD budget, and it will be available to cover unbudgeted costs in other areas,” said Ann Gorman, a central staff analyst. “Perhaps SFD will need funding in some other areas that haven’t been identified, and unneeded overtime costs will just be shifted into those accounts.”

Budget Chair Dan Strauss chose to include the larger $7.1 million SFD overtime addition to his balancing package released this week, potentially allowing SFD access to $2 million they are unlikely to use for overtime.

SPD got into hot water back in 2012 when the Seattle City Council learned that the department had obtained two unmanned aerial drones via a federal homeland security grant they received in 2010. SPD hadn’t kept the council informed about their plans to use the drones even though they’d already started training officers in their usage. At that time, the department hadn’t drafted any policies around usage of the drones. A public outcry led to the SPD abandoning their drone plans, and the ACLU took the opportunity to ask the City for a surveillance ordinance.

A surveillance equipment ordinance was passed in 2013 , but that wasn’t the end of the saga. Instead, SPD secretly purchased social media tracking software in 2014, which, when discovered in 2016, the department said wasn’t covered under the surveillance equipment ordinance because it was software, not hardware. This episode ultimately led to the council passing a new, revamped surveillance ordinance in 2017 .

More recently, two audits released earlier this year showed further overreach on SPD’s part. In the last year, SPD integrated several unapproved Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) traffic camera feeds into its real-time crime center. While SPD failed to adopt a formal policy around how it would integrate private cameras into its real-time crime center, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) also found SPD has trouble following its own camera masking requirements for private areas viewed by its cameras due to the lack of availability of technicians.
Now questions have arisen about SPD’s usage of aerial drones, which originally led to Seattle having a surveillance ordinance and is still not allowed.
However, the King County Sheriff's Office (KCSO) has a fleet of drones that can fly into Seattle to help SPD, whether that be for large events like World Cup games or after emergencies.

“We have concerns that KCSO drones flying over Seattle enables SPD to essentially bypass the Seattle surveillance ordinance and the protections it is intended to provide,” said Tee Sannon, ACLU-WA’s technology policy program director. “Without proper regulation, drones pose a serious threat to people's privacy and civil liberties. They can carry multiple surveillance tools that capture data about people and their movements without their knowledge or consent, which could potentially chill free speech and impinge on people's free association rights. For law enforcement agencies seeking to use tools like drones, the use must be carefully regulated to minimize these threats from surveillance, such as by placing strict limits on what data they can collect, how long it can be retained, how it can be used, and who it can be shared with.”

Records shared with The Urbanist by Rose Terse show that in spite of not being allowed to use drones due to the surveillance ordinance, SPD was directly involved in applying for a federal grant to fund a regional drone program. During her time employed at SPD, Carrie Martin née Chitty, then the Regional Law Enforcement Homeland Security Program Manager for the SPD Metropolitan Safety Services Bureau, played a significant role in pulling together a regional drone proposal in 2020 that received money from the Homeland Security Grant Program in 2021.

Martin communicated with several local law enforcement agencies about their drone programs and convened a meeting with members of the Everett and Renton Police Departments to discuss the regional drone program and identify “a lead agency” for the grant proposal.
After the project successfully received the grant, Martin (then Chitty) explained her continuing role to Renton Police Department’s Commander Charles Karlewicz on April 1, 2021.

“The Fy21 UASI sUAS project was funded at $100,000!!! Super exciting,” Martin wrote. “I am going to be working with Deputy Chris Pelczar from KCSO TAC30 on developing the Regional deployment plan for the equipment that will be purchased with the grant funding.”
Martin is now employed as a grants administrator at KCSO, and SPD has benefited from the culmination of the regional drone project she helped bring about, often “borrowing” one of KCSO’s drones.

“It's pretty common for the SWAT team to borrow the drone for deployments where you have a barricaded armed subject,” SPD Captain James Britt told The Urbanist during a tour of the real-time crime center in 2025. “We have a great relationship with our friends over at the Sheriff's Office in their TAC 30 unit. It's common for the SWAT team to do it. It's not common beyond that.”
According to The Seattle Times , both Seattle IT and the OIG’s Inspector General for Public Safety Lisa Judge agree that the surveillance ordinance doesn’t apply when SPD calls in KCSO’s drones.
“The City can’t enforce its surveillance ordinance on other jurisdictions,” Dan Pitts, audit supervisor at the OIG, told The Urbanist .
Communities Not Cameras, a local grassroots organization that opposes surveillance, says the distinction lies in which agency is directing the activity of the drones.

“KCSO operating drones in Seattle is not, per se, a violation of that ordinance,” the group wrote to The Urbanist . “When Seattle Police direct that use, outside of exigent circumstances, they are doing so in violation of the law.”

Communities Not Cameras pointed out that in 2021, SPD submitted a Surveillance Impact Report for helicopters with infrared cameras, which was a tool they were borrowing from KCSO, and the council adopted it by ordinance.

“Drones should go through the same process. A rule that applies only to equipment SPD owns is not oversight. It is a procurement rule,” Communities Not Cameras wrote. “If borrowing exempts a tool, any technology the Council has rejected or never reviewed is one phone call away, including license plate readers, cell site simulators, and facial recognition held by neighboring agencies. Mutual aid exists for emergencies. It should not become a standing workaround for public review.”

Communities Not Cameras would like the council to amend the ordinance to state plainly that it covers any surveillance technology used at the request of, or on behalf of, a City department, regardless of who owns or operates it. They also want to include a requirement that SPD report every mutual aid request involving surveillance technology.

“The spirit, if not the letter, of the law already prohibits the department from acquiring and using drone technology through a third-party like KCSO,” Communities Not Cameras wrote. “There is just no appetite on the City’s side to enforce it.”

On the SFD side, in June, The Seattle Times reported that an AI technology had been assisting SFD 911 dispatchers since 2023 in deciding which callers would get a rapid response and which would be referred to a nurse-staffed call center in Texas. SFD has been using the AI tool, provided by the Danish company Corti, without any disclosure to the public or any evaluations of efficacy, safety, or data privacy.
Ryan Calo, a University of Washington law professor and co-director of the university’s Tech Policy Lab, shared his concerns with The Urbanist .

“People have the right to know if AI is being used to make consequential decisions such as who should be fast tracked and who should be sent on an alternative track,” Calo said. “More specifically, if you’re a person who has been sent to the nurse’s line or an alternative path because AI suggested it and you get hurt or don’t get the care you expect, you should know AI is involved. I don’t like the fact it was hidden from the public.”
Calo said he didn’t like the idea of a third party listening into 911 calls without notice.

Recent reporting from The Seattle Times uncovered a 2019 internal privacy risk analysis memo written by Ginger Armbruster, then Seattle’s chief privacy officer, which revealed concerns about data ownership and sharing, data breaches, and equity.
In September, when Kettle invited SFD leadership to a public safety committee meeting to discuss the issue, SFD Chief Harold Scoggins defended the department’s use of the Corti AI tool.
“All of our dispatchers are firefighter EMTs. They have all worked in our system,” Scoggins said.

articles.title: Nilu Jenks Wins Seattle Council Seat in Blowout
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Nilu Jenks has won a Seattle City Council seat based on the decisive 17-point lead she ran up on election night. That lead is likely to grow as more votes are counted in coming days, since last-minute votes lean progressive in Seattle. Jenks' lead held steady in Wednesday's ballot drop .

A progressive advocate, Jenks led the nonprofit FairVote Washington, which fought for the ranked-choice voting reform that is going into effect in Seattle municipal elections next year. She also ran for city council in 2023 and finished third in the primary, trailing centrist Cathy Moore and ChrisTiana ObeySumner, whom The Stranger endorsed. The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve) endorsed Jenks in that 2023 race and again in 2026 .

After victory became apparent Tuesday, Jenks told The Urbanist that safety-focused designs of Aurora Avenue N and Lake City Way were among her top priorities. Aurora has a $50 million state grant earmarked for it, but state lawmakers like Seattle Rep. Julia Reed have grown impatient with the slow pace of getting the project shovel-ready.

"I would love to get the money allocated for Aurora moving and actually really get more, so that we can make Aurora a place that everybody gets to enjoy from bikers and walkers, and have good dedicated bus lanes, but also so that you can go to those businesses along there that deserve our support," Jenks said. "I also want to get similar funds for Lake City Way. It's another area where a lot of people get hit, and you know, it's not safe for pedestrians."

At an election night gathering of supporters at Mojito in North Seattle, Jenks framed her apparent victory as part of the larger battle to stop Trumpism, restore faith in American institutions, and lower the cost of living.

"As the daughter of Iranian immigrants, I know democracy is not something we can take for granted," Jenks said in her election night speech. "I grew up watching my parents lose their country, and as an Iranian American, I watch an ever-looming threat of war hang over the country my family came from while families here at home face fear, uncertainty, and rising costs. Trump's war with Iran has cost billions of dollars, with rising fuel prices adding pressure to household budgets."
With Democrats winning the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's blue wave election, pressure to end the Iran war will be ramping up.

Meanwhile, Jenks' win will shift the balance of power on Seattle City Council, growing the progressive bloc to four members. The remaining five members sometimes form a centrist bloc, although D6's Dan Strauss and D1's Rob Saka sometimes vote with progressives. Flipping the D5 seat from centrists to progressives will give Mayor Katie Wilson an easier time moving her legislation. Moreover, it will remove interim Councilmember Debora Juarez, who had been one of the mayor's harshest critics, especially on public safety issues .

Jenks has a different approach to public safety than Juarez or Moore, emphasizing the need to expand the civilian-run Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department. When The Urbanist asked which issues she would seek to lead at council, Jenks brought up expanding CARE, tackling food deserts, and adding incentives for heat pumps as a way to shrink energy bills and the city's climate footprint.

"I am really excited to figure out food deserts and how we can solve that problem," Jenks said. "I would love to work to expand the CARE team. Get us a police chief that loves this city, and will be collaborative with an alternative response team, and ideally has worked with one before. I am excited to work on trying to figure out on-bill financing for heat pumps to stabilize our heat grid."

In winning her seat, Jenks defeated Julie Kang, an educator and former bank chair who had backing from centrist leaders in the District 5 special election. Councilmembers Bob Kettle and Maritza Rivera endorsed Kang, as did former Councilmembers Sara Nelson and Tim Burgess, who also donated to a political action committee (PAC) backing her. Current Council President Joy Hollingsworth endorsed both Jenks and Kang.

The drubbing Kang took appears as a warning sign and a repudiation for those centrists as they face their own elections next year, when all seven district-based council seats are up. D5's seat was up in an even-year special election due to Cathy Moore's decision to resign before her term was up. Jenks will assume office as soon as election results are certified later this month, rather than waiting until January, but she'll also face reelection next year.
In her speech, Jenks emphasized that she saw that District 5 residents were facing struggles and she intended to do something about it.

"I see the person who can't afford a car or the unbelievable gas prices and who relies on public transit and protected bike lanes to get around their city," Jenks said. "I see the immigrant family and the young trans person who wants what we all want: to feel safe, loved, and free to be themselves – to build a future here, and know their city will stand by them."

Another campaign focus for Jenks was food security and access, which became a hot button issue when grocery giant Kroger announced the closure of the Lake City Fred Meyer store upon which many community members had relied.

"I see the grocery store working hard for fair wages and also for accessible food in our neighborhoods. Thank you. I see the senior on a fixed income wondering whether they can afford to stay in the city they helped build as rent, housing, and property taxes keep rising," Jenks said. "I see the small business owner who has poured everything into their business and wants a safe, thriving neighborhood where they can succeed in a city that helps them instead of getting in their way, and I see the parent who wants their child to walk home safely in a city that responds to public safety with both urgency and compassion. These are the people behind this campaign, and these are the people I'm going to carry with me to City Hall."

To defeat Trump's campaigns of hate and corruption, Jenks argued Seattle must be a shining city on a hill and provide a beacon of light showing progressive leadership in big cities is able to deliver. Urbanist touchstones of high-quality transit, connected sidewalks, and abundant housing were a key part of the image Jenks invoked during her campaign, illustrating why she won The Urbanist's endorsement this year (and in 2023, for that matter). Bus improvements will be much more feasible with the passage of the Seattle Transit Measure, which ran up a huge lead in election night returns.

"That's what this moment demands of us: not that we stop being afraid, but that we refuse to let our fear decide who we become," Jenks said. "Across this country, Trump and his allies tell us our cities are broken, that the answer is more fear, more division, and more crackdowns. But Seattle is choosing another path. Once every vote counted, it's time to deliver. Our cities have to show they can govern, not someday, now. When we can't build housing, fix a sidewalk, or keep a bus stop safe, we make the argument for the people who say our cities don't work. So let's prove them wrong by making this city work for all of us."

articles.title: ‘Big noodle culture’ — RUAM brings Thai bowls, noodles, and new energy to Capitol Hill’s 15th Ave E
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: RUAM won’t save 15th Ave E on its own but it’s a healthy sign the soul of the Capitol Hill-top neighborhood is intact despite challenges.

The newly opened Thai restaurant is focused: noodle soups, dry noodles, and rice bowls that fill shops across Thailand. Owner Thisun Polasub says it’s a side of Thai cuisine that rarely gets its own spotlight in Seattle.
There is no pad thai on the menu at RUAM, by design.

“When we talk about Thai food, people just think of one category,” Polasub tells CHS. “But if you talk about Japanese food, there’s a dedicated sushi restaurant. There’s katsu. There’s ramen. In Thailand, we have a big noodle culture, and I want to highlight that.”
RUAM is Polasub’s second restaurant. His first, Thai Rhapsody in Mill Creek, serves traditional dishes most diners expect: pad thai, pad see ew, fried rice. For Capitol Hill, he wanted a new concept.
“This one is totally different,” he said. “We don’t have pad thai. We don’t have fried rice.”
The restaurant veteran is candid about the risk. Opening on 15th Ave E is “totally different water” than Mill Creek, with a very different cost structure. The investment has kept him up at night.
“This is quite a big bet,” he said. “But I want to offer the best thing I can do for my customers. I believe if I do good, people will see it, and they will come and support.”
That energy is needed on the strip where a long wait for redevelopment on a core block of 15th Ave E has come with the closure of several neighborhood spaces.

CHS reported in September on the sudden closure of Rione XIII, Rubinstein Bagels, and Bar Vacilando as structural issues and landlord problems have emptied the 96-year-old building where they made their home at 15th and Harrison.

2026 has also left the former Ada’s Technical Books shuttered but new businesses are joining the area including a rebirth of Bar Cantinetta and delayed but still in motion plans for Fire Tacos & Cantina to join 15th in the old Coastal Kitchen building.

Looming around it all is the on-hold six-story redevelopment of the street’s old QFC block as local developer Hunters Capital keeps the stretch busy with pop-up businesses while waiting out the challenging economic conditions that have put new construction mostly on ice across the city.

The street continues to welcome new openings like the addition of Ha Ha Coffee this fall. Losses continue, too, like Club Comedy Seattle that failed to find a buyer and shuttered in the street level space below where RUAM has opened up.
RUAM itself is replacing a recent 15th Ave E closure. Bites of Bangkok shuttered after a seven-year run in the space. The restaurant space was home to Capitol Hill’s much-loved Bagel Deli .

For Polasub, RUAM’s focus is personal. Noodles came to Thailand from China, he said, and the country’s large Chinese immigrant community helped make them part of everyday life. He grew up eating soup noodles, dry noodles and simple rice bowls topped with chicken or pork.
“That’s the food every Thai person grows up with,” he said. “It’s my favorite.”

At RUAM, those noodle-shop staples get dressed up. Where a street vendor in Thailand might serve beef noodles with whatever cut is on hand, RUAM uses ribeye. Dishes come topped with fried enoki mushrooms and microgreens. Some bowls swap in Japanese udon for traditional rice noodles. The menu also includes Pink Velvet Yen Ta Fo, a version of Thailand’s well-known pink noodle soup, served with crispy seafood.
“The look is modernized, but the taste stays true to bold, authentic Thai flavor,” Polasub said.

The restaurant’s signature dish is the ribeye Jaew Hon, an aromatic, herb-heavy soup from Thailand’s northeastern Isaan region. The kitchen makes the sauce in house from lemongrass, galangal and other herbs. Polasub says it’s the dish every first-time visitor should order.
He remembers the first time he tasted the finished version, a few days after opening.
“I slurped that hot soup and it just blew my mind,” he said. “I didn’t think it would taste that good.”

The menu comes from executive chef and manager Scott Wisitkran , who runs RUAM day to day. Wisitkran grew up cooking in his parents’ restaurant in Thailand before moving to Sydney, Australia in 2012 where he worked his way up through kitchens to become a head chef. He came to Seattle in 2017 and has worked in Thai and other Asian restaurants around the area since.

Polasub says he gives Wisitkran full creative control. “I give him freedom because I know how good he is,” he said. The two do adjust recipes together, along with Polasub’s wife, who runs Thai Rhapsody and who he says has a gift for knowing exactly what a dish is missing.

Most of RUAM’s ingredients are sourced locally. Polasub says herbs that were hard to find in the U.S. 10 or 15 years ago are now grown in Florida and Mexico and easy to get here. Only a few specialty items are imported from Thailand.

The name RUAM means “together” in Thai. Polasub says he chose a name that people who don’t speak Thai could still pronounce, and one that captured what he wants the restaurant to be: a place where people gather over good food. He picked the location for its mix of a quieter, walkable Capitol Hill street with parking out front.
“We gather, we simmer it, and you savor it,” he said.
Polasub says he reads customer feedback closely and passes it along to the kitchen so the team can keep improving. “I really care about my customers,” he said. “I want people to leave happy.”
So far, the early signs are encouraging. Polasub says RUAM started slow and quiet while staffing settled in, but has already started to collect five-star reviews from customers.
He admits he obsessed over the details of the space, changing the design several times.“My wife reminded me, ‘Honey, you are not building a museum,’” he said.
RUAM is located at 340 15th Ave E. Learn more at r uamkitchen.com .

articles.title: With early returns showing little room for I-638 ‘No’ flip, advocates prepare for court battle
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: While initial election returns show Washington voters approving Initiative 638 , LGBTQ+ civil rights advocates emphasize that there are still votes to count, holding out hope as hundreds of thousands of drop-box and mail-in ballots continue to be tabulated across the state. They are also preparing to battle the measure in court.

The Capitol Hill-based Gender Justice League offered an urgent assessment of the measure, which restricts transgender girls from competing in K–12 female sports categories and requires biological sex verification for all female student-athletes.

“I-638 was sold as a rule about a handful of Trans youth, when in reality, it’s a medical sex check for every girl playing school sports in this state — whether Trans or not,” a statement from the organization said.

The organization said it is readying to support plans to challenge the law in court alongside coalition partners if the vote holds, while noting that late funding hindered broad grassroots voter education.

A flip faces challenging math. Statewide, the “Yes” campaign holds a 291,722-vote advantage as of Thursday morning. With an estimated 600,000 to 900,000 ballots left to count across Washington, the “No” campaign needs roughly 63% to 74% of all outstanding ballots to reverse the lead.
In King County, the state’s primary progressive bastion and one of only a few counties where “No” is ahead, the measure has generated 57.25% against it so far.

With the likelihood that the vote holds, the next focus will be on making sure the ban can’t be put in place. In a statement, the ACLU of Washington said it will “never waver in its commitment to transgender people and their right to exist as their full selves, and we will explore all potential next steps to uphold the rights of transgender girls and their access to school sports.”

“Transgender youth are our neighbors, children, friends and family, and like everyone, they have the right to live and play in our communities as their true selves,” the organization’s statement concluded.

Community organizers including GEM Seattle are mobilizing for a rally and march at Westlake Park Thursday night. Demonstrators will gather to demand the protection of transgender youth, plan next steps, and celebrate the historic election of Jaelynn Scott , Washington’s first openly trans state legislator who will represent the 37th District including South Seattle.

articles.title: Seattle wins $9.7 million federal grant to overhaul high-crash streets and signals
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A federal award in 2023 helped create this Capitol Hill crosswalk at Harvard and E Olive Way — two years later

The City of Seattle has received a $9.7 million federal Safe Streets and Roads for All grant from the U.S. Department of Transportation to fund targeted traffic safety improvements and accident prevention.
While no projects are designated for Capitol Hill or the Central District, the funding targets key travel corridors and intersections with severe crash histories.

A major portion of the funds will pay for skid-resistant road surfacing at four crash-prone corridors: Rainier Avenue South, Westlake Avenue North, Highland Park Way Southwest, and Southwest Roxbury Street. According to federal safety data, this pavement treatment can cut wet-weather crashes by up to 83%.

The grant also finances rebuilt traffic signals at two busy intersections bordering Pioneer Square and the Chinatown–International District: 4th Ave S at S Jackson and at South Main. These upgrades will give pedestrians longer head starts before vehicle traffic gets a green light and will prioritize emergency vehicles.
Finally, the city will use the funds to conduct a citywide crash analysis covering 15 years of data. That study will guide future safety investments across all neighborhoods.

articles.title: Altura makes its Broadway crossing: bigger space, same staff, and a deeper connection to another Capitol Hill chef great
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Before this fall gets away from us — and before its old space goes back into motion with a new concept, CHS should mark a milestone on Broadway. Altura has completed its move across the street into the space where its sister restaurant Carrello grew.

Remarkably, chef and owner Nathan Lockwood has brought everyone along. All employees from both Altura and Carrello have kept their jobs through the transition, according to the restaurant’s announcement. The combined team is working together in the new space, which operates six days a week from Tuesday through Sunday.

Also remarkably, Altura has expanded from its original 1,500-square-foot footprint into the 7,500-square-foot restaurant space on the east side of Broadway without bloating what has made it award worthy. Instead of using the 6,000 square feet of added room to scale up the dining room, Lockwood kept the core tasting menu service intimate by adding just five seats compared to the old dining room. Tasting menu seatings are scheduled for 5:30 PM Tuesday through Thursday and Sunday, with two seatings at 5:15 PM and 8:15 PM on Fridays and Saturdays.

The rest of the expanded footprint is dedicated to the spirit of Carrello with lounge and garden patio spaces. These areas take on Carrello’s à la carte format, serving antipasti, handmade pasta, plated entrées, and desserts. The lounge and patio also host Aperitivo Hour featuring Italian drinks paired with food. In addition, Carrello’s wooden service carts have been kept over, rolling tableside to deliver cheese, caviar, and dessert courses.

The family merger means diners who may not want to stretch for the $195 a pop tasting menu can still enjoy the Altura experience with a $95/person “feast for the table” or the a la carte menu’s $20-$35 antipasti, pasta dishes, or special entrees. Fish and meat cuts from the restaurant’s “whole animal butchery program” run between $40 and $65.

Establishing it as one of Seattle’s premier tasting menu destinations through multiple James Beard Award honors and top rankings across the city’s food and drink media, Lockwood opened Altura on the west side of Broadway in October 2011, transforming the space of a former art and furniture boutique.

Altura’s new side of the street also connects Lockwood’s award winning restaurant to another Capitol Hill chef great. The new Altura space was previously home to the legendary 11-year run of Poppy from James Beard-honored chef Jerry Traunfeld .
With their fall move completed, Lockwood and team are now looking forward to the holidays and hosting their Feast of Seven Fishes for Christmas Eve as well as hosting diners on New Year’s Eve.
Altura is now located at 622 Broadway E. Learn more at alturarestaurant.com .

articles.title: Slog AM: Washington Bans Trans Girls from Girls Sports, the “World’s Largest Jew-Hater” Is Investigating Antisemitism at UW, and More Nuclear Weapons Are Bound for Our Shores
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: The Ayatollah responds to the blue wave: “If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they’re gravely mistaken,” he posted on X. While Democrats won big Tuesday off Trump’s unpopular war, Iranians, like much of the world downrange of the US, are waiting for the rugpull.

The US is still arming a genocide, and one new congressman has seen it up close: US Representative-elect Adam Hamawy of New Jersey says what he saw in Gaza volunteering as a surgeon made him run for office. “After coming back from Gaza. I just couldn’t go back to life as usual, because what I witnessed there wasn’t a war. I witnessed a level of destruction I had never experienced before. What I witnessed was really a genocide. I was taking care of the victims of it, and I couldn’t stay silent,” he told Democracy Now in June.

Here in the weapons factory we call Seattle, the agenda is more bombs: Two major military expansions are planned for the Salish Sea, a “mega” drydock for US Navy repairs, as well as eight new ballistic missile submarines for the Navy’s quiet nuclear weapons complex on the Kitsap Peninsula. These submarines aren’t the type that torpedo other ships, they’re the worldenders that lurk in the dark corners of the Earth waiting for the signal to nuke millions of civilian foreigners at a moments notice.

Israel thrilled by new Congressional Democratic leadership: Yair Lapid, the far-right leader of the Israeli legislature’s opposition to the far-right Likudnik-led governing coalition, posted the following on X, the everything app: “Hakeem Jeffries will lead the House of Representatives. Chuck Schumer will run the Senate. Both are my friends; both voted with Israel this year even when the majority of their party caucus voted otherwise.”

“The world’s largest Jew-hater,” that’s how the chair of the DOJ’s Task Force to Combat Anti-Semitism described Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who launched the DOJ’s recent investigation into the University of Washington, according to an investigation by the Harvard Crimson. The UW administrators who smeared their students as antisemitic find themselves in strange company, and out on a limb after Tuesday’s election results. To shamelessly plug my own work, you can read The Stranger’s new comprehensive coverage of the prosecution of 33 UW students who occupied a Boeing-sponsored campus building last year.

Washington voters ban trans girls from trans sports: I-638, the far-right-sponsored public initiative, has passed, and as of latest vote totals it wasn’t even close, 57-43. Voters in most counties supported the ban, and opponents didn’t pick up enough votes in the counties that recognize bigotry for what it is (like King County). Expect a human rights lawsuit to accomplish what Washington voters were too stupid to do. In the meantime, the Gender Equity Movement has organized a rally and march set for 6 p.m. tonight at Westlake Park if you need somewhere to scream.

I don’t read the Seattle Times business section for its coverage of social justice and historical inequity, but I do think their recent coverage of the wealthy Freeman family’s latest real-estate listing in Bellevue could have written more than the following: “The grandfather’s history is controversial, however. He agitated for decades for the exclusion of Japanese immigrants, including the farmers working the strawberry fields that covered the Eastside.”

Miller Freeman was an ardent anti-Asian racist, not just an agitator for “exclusion,” but for deportation of the Japanese-American community to concentration camps during the war. He fought to keep them from returning as well. Freeman’s reputation is so bad among the Japanese-American community that Densho, the digital archive and public history center devoted to documenting America’s wartime concentration camps, has a whole section on him. It’s crucial context.

Some good news from the Times that flew under the radar: The five Washington immigrants snatched at night from a family camping trip in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest have been released from Tacoma’s ICE camp, the Northwest ICE Processing Center. The Seattle Times coverage here is refreshingly comprehensive.

“Accountability is coming,” says Minnesota Governor on visit to Renee Good and Alex Pretti’s memorial: Residents have been covering the memorial to the ICE victims with “I voted” stickers for the past few days, with heartbreaking photos available from Minnesota Public Radio. We will see if voting is enough.

Before accountability, profit: If you can stomach it, Politico has a rundown of Democrat-oriented K Street lobbyists absolutely salivating at the business opportunities presented by the blue tsunami in the US Senate. Just how big of a night was it for reptile class? “ONE OF K STREET’S OWN: Adrian Boafo, who until recently worked as a senior director of government affairs for Oracle, was elected to replace outgoing Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) last night, Daniel B. reports. It marks a rare case of a lobbyist being elected to Congress,” Politico reports.

The feds say they caught the fake anthrax mail attack suspect: They say the man, arrested in Oklahoma City (a city no stranger to actual terror attacks) was responsible for a similar stunt back in 2024, the Associated Press reports . Rather than a DSA guy, as the return address on the mail falsely tried to present, the suspect is just another MAGA boomer.

I know I probably got you down after your post-election high, but here is your reward: Rod Crawford, “Curator of Arachnids” at the Burke Museum, and Washington’s leading spider man, has a lot to say about your Halloween spider decorations. God bless our cranks.

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): Aries psychologist Abraham Maslow coined the term “peak experiences”: surging upflows of heightened clarity, awe, vitality, and love. He also identified another category, “plateau experiences.” These are gentler but more enduring states, characterized less by ecstatic fireworks than by a leisurely delight in being alive. I believe you’re in a phase that favors those plateau experiences. So the semi-bad news is that you may not be besieged by a nonstop flood of spectacular epiphanies. The good news is that you’ll harvest a steady stream of subtle amazements. Your gratitude may be less dramatic but more sustained. A calm, glowing contentment can teach you all you need to know right now.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): A finely crafted mechanical watch depends upon many gears moving at different speeds. Some spin rapidly, while others barely move. Yet each contributes to the overall success of timekeeping. Please remember this when you get restless about your uneven progress. Not every area of your life can or should be in dynamic motion simultaneously. One project may require vigorous action while another benefits from patient incubation. A single standard of productivity isn’t right for you these days. Harmonious coordination among different rhythms serves you best.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): I invite you and urge you to ruminate about the stories you’ve been telling about yourself. Are they still accurate? Still empowering? Or have some become outdated myths that no longer honor your ripening identity? During the coming weeks, I predict you will be energized as you revise your personal mythology with imaginative generosity. It’s time to retire narratives that shrink you. Reinvent an old saga so it makes you more of a hero and less of a victim. Compose two fun new tales that are spacious enough to accommodate the curious beauty you’re on your way to becoming.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): Among elephants, older matriarchs lead the herd. They carry detailed memories of watering holes, migration routes, and old brushes with danger. During tough times, their accumulated experience becomes indispensable. This fact of nature reminds me that your own history contains wisdom you haven’t fully appreciated. And now is an excellent phase to bring it all into your conscious awareness. Instead of dwelling on old disappointments or sad mistakes, focus intensely on what durable knowledge you’ve harvested from living through them. Your future and the futures of those you care for will improve in direct proportion to the respect you show your past. The point is to recognize yourself as an increasingly skillful keeper of hard-earned sagacity.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): A bird doesn’t perceive reflective glass as we do. To it, the spotless glass façade of a building may look like a continuation of the outdoors, with blue sky, clouds, tree canopy, or water. But humans have the know-how to create bird-friendly patterns that interrupt this illusion by giving the glass enough visual “texture” to register as a solid obstacle. With these visual clues, birds are less likely to collide with the structure. In the coming weeks, Leo, I hope you will summon comparable thoughtfulness. Your small gestures can protect others from unnecessary confusion or pain. You’ll have extra power to express subtle kindnesses that free people to navigate the world more safely and confidently.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): You may be feeling so physically well right now that it seems almost implausible. Your mind may be operating so sharply that you wonder whether you can trust it. Even love may appear so straightforward and righteous that part of you suspects you have misunderstood the signs. But that’s the cosmic joke: These blessings don’t come with an invoice or a looming punishment. You’re allowed to receive them freely. Tell your harsh inner critic that its counsel isn’t needed. Then make ample room for the release and freedom that are unfolding.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): I’m not right 100 percent of the time, but even when I’m not completely correct, I usually get close to at least one of the key truths simmering in your story. In the oracle you’re reading now, I’m offering a concise burst of guidance that I believe is even more likely than usual to be 100 percent accurate. I’m urging you to examine the balance of give-and-take in one specific relationship. Your gift for harmony can sometimes tip into always being the one who accommodates, adjusts, and gives more, until the scales sit lopsided and you barely notice. Investigate that possibility, please. Fixing the imbalance is an act of care for a bond that’s worth keeping healthy.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): How long has it been since you’ve meandered around a library? I’m old-fashioned about books, so that experience is high on my list of pleasurable adventures. I enjoy searching for specific books but I also love browsing the shelves without a fixed destination. Both approaches are valuable, though browsing often produces happy surprises. One unexpected title leads to another, opening pathways no search engine could have predicted. With this in mind, Scorpio, I recommend that you browse freely in the coming weeks. Wander through ideas, friendships, music, bookstores, museums, forests, conversations, and neighborhoods without demanding a predetermined outcome. Serendipity is preparing a curriculum especially suited to restless brilliance.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): There’s a Welsh word, hiraeth , that refers to a longing for a home that may never have existed. It’s a homesickness for a place or a way of being you can’t actually return to and aren’t sure was ever fully real. I bring this up, Sagittarius, because I suspect you’re feeling the tug of distant horizons lately, a restless ache for an elsewhere you can’t name. Don’t dismiss this longing as mere wanderlust to be scratched with a plane ticket. Sit with it. Ask what it’s pointing toward. The far country you ache for may be a quality of soul you’re being called to cultivate right where you are. Your true destination might be more interior than you assume.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): Engineers who design a suspension bridge know the structure must be able to sway slightly in wind and weather. A perfectly rigid structure would eventually crack under stress. In the coming weeks, I’m hoping you’ll incorporate extra doses of this paradoxical attitude. It’s crucial not just to grudgingly acknowledge but to fondly celebrate the fact that stability will thrive on generous flexibility. Some plans and convictions will grow even stronger because you’ll be willing to adjust and tinker with them.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Astronomers sometimes revisit old telescope data using improved software. In doing so, they may discover planets or galaxies that had been hidden from them for years. The information was always there. Only the methods of perception changed. I suspect you’re ripe for similar types of revelation, Aquarius. I invite you to return to old notebooks, abandoned ideas, neglected friendships, or forgotten ambitions. You may not have extracted all their value yet. Your present self possesses interpretive abilities that your former self lacked. Yesterday’s overlooked clue may be tomorrow’s breakthrough.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): Nineteenth-century Piscean composer and pianist Frédéric Chopin poured an almost unbearable tenderness into his nocturnes and preludes. His delicate, intimate music is among the most emotional ever created. Evoking potent, mysterious feelings was his specialty. I propose we make him your inspirational role model. Please do everything you can imagine to express your deep feelings with artistry and intelligence. Be as sensitive and impassioned as you dare.
Homework: What’s your secret for enhancing your capacity to give and receive love ?

articles.title: Wednesday’s Ballot Drop Is Here
articles.author: Stranger Election Control Board
paras: We have more ballots and more votes! But not many. For any big, or really any noticeable, changes, we’ll have to wait for tomorrow’s ballot drop and Friday’s. Those will have a trove of election day ballots. But here’s what’s up.

We’ve got our eye on whether Dems win a supermajority in the state House, where their majority before the election sat at 59-39. They need 66 for a supermajority, so seven wins, but until we get bigger ballot drops later in the week it’s a tough call to make.

One of the more interesting of the districts that could flip to the Democrats is over in the Yakima Valley, and which didn’t get much attention this year (outside these parts). As of the latest ballot drop from Yakima County, two Democratic challengers to the long Republican rule in LD 14 have increased their margins slightly. Challenger Chelsea Dimas now leads Republican incumbent Rep. Gloria Mendoza by about 11 points, and Democrat Ezequiel Morfin now leads Rep. Deb Manjarrez by 12 points. LD 14 is awkwardly drawn due to court orders meant to empower Latino voters in one of the few communities where they are in the majority in Washington, meaning votes have to be counted in this week across four counties before we know if farmworker-aligned Dems will usurp Republicans who represent the interests of the planters.

Republicans gave mixed signals last night on their chances of victory in the 14th. Manjarrez told the Yakima Herald-Republic last night that she is “very disappointed” and “wanted to keep representing my district,” while state GOP Chair Jim Walsh said the 14th was a district Republicans expect to “grind out wins.”

Back to the center of the universe—King County—around 65,000 new ballots have worked their way into the vote totals. This is a pathetic little drop compared to what’s to come tomorrow and Friday (bigger, heftier ballot drops). Right now, King County Elections has voter turnout pegged at 55.5 percent, but according to spokesperson Halei Watkins, that number is expected to climb as they keep processing ballots.

There is really nothing up in the air exclusively in King County, however. Rebecca Saldaña continues to trounce Toshiko Hasegawa for the pleasure of representing King County Council District 2. Rep. Gerry Pollet is domming Will Dreher in North Seattle. And the voters clearly didn’t like nurse Ashley Fedan enough to boot out Israel apologist David Hackney, who is running away with it in the 11th LD. Rep. Amy Walen is still losing to Jessica Forsythe for opposing the Millionaires Tax. LD 32 is split between King and Snohomish counties, and as of now, Rep. Cyndy Ryu is still winning the race to unseat Sen. Jesse Salomon by a few hundred votes, and Danica Noble is still ahead of Keith Scully for the House rep slot. This is all Democrat-on-Democrat violence.

If only we alone could decide the fate of the terrible anti-trans ballot initiative. Have you looked at the Seattle Times map of the voting data? We here in King County are an island of “no” on that issue in a sea of transphobia (although shoutout to Jefferson County, whose small population voted against transphobia at a higher rate than us).

On that note, the trans sports ban initiative has stayed mostly the same—the yes votes are still leading. The Millionaires Tax repeal is still sucking rocks and so is the revival of the Parents’ Bill of Rights.
