articles.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
articles.author:
<name>Christine Slaughter, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Boston University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christine-slaughter-1538458"/>
paras: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals , as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black .

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results . Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms , up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.
In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes , which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County .
In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3% , from 50.6% in 2020 , as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide , Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll .

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed . NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson , who won the governorship over Republican John James.
Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.
Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate .

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity . Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination . If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.
My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program , while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience . El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election . Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.
“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

articles.title: How Amendment 3, vaccine mandates and school vouchers will shape Florida under the leadership of Byron Donalds
articles.author:
<name>Liv Coleman, Professor of Political Science and International Studies, University of Tampa</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/liv-coleman-2758243"/>
paras: In the midst of what pundits are calling a blue tsunami nationwide , Florida remained resolutely red , electing Republican Byron Donalds as its first Black governor and sending Republican Ashley Moody back to the U.S. Senate.
Donalds ran on a promise to continue the legacy of his predecessor , Gov. Ron DeSantis.

His victory was not as easily won as polls had predicted . In the week leading up to the election, polls put him at 4 points over his opponent, Democrat David Jolly. In the end, Donalds won by 1.3 points – about 107,000 votes.

I’m a political scientist who has lived in Florida for almost two decades and seen the powers of the governor’s office grow. We can see based on Donalds’ campaign promises the direction in which he plans to lead the state.
Donalds’ term as governor will start with a major change: On Nov. 3, Floridians voted to pass Amendment 3 to the state constitution.
This will cause a shift in the state’s long-standing commitment to home rule , the principle that local governments, such as cities and counties, should be able to set policy on local issues.

The amendment limits local government spending from tax revenue to core categories such as public safety, schools and natural resources. With a lower tax base, some local governments in rural areas may not be able to maintain basic services and might need help from the state.
DeSantis has called for a special session to address Amendment 3 before Donalds takes office.
DeSantis has said he plans to restrict home rule by stopping local governments from trying to raise revenue through additional taxation at the local level .
Donalds supported the amendment , and it will give him and the Legislature the opportunity to redistribute tax funding throughout the state.

This election has changed the makeup of the state Legislature, though, with the GOP losing its supermajority in the Florida House of Representatives, which requires holding 80 out of the 120 seats. This change in the Legislature could make it more difficult for Donalds to control the agenda in Tallahassee the way DeSantis did during his second term, when he had a supermajority in both houses of the Legislature.

Donalds has affirmed that he supports the big steps DeSantis has taken to limit home rule – such as limiting local control over land development and removing local elected officials from office – and plans to take executive authority further , scheduling more DOGE audits of local government and removing more elected officials as he sees fit.
When it comes to data centers, on the other hand, Donalds has said he favors local communities deciding whether to allow them to be built nearby.

One of the first choices awaiting Donalds will be whom to appoint as Florida surgeon general, a position created in 2007 . The position comes with the power to declare public health emergencies , forcibly quarantine people and set vaccine mandates for illnesses such as chickenpox that fall outside the state Legislature’s framework of seven childhood vaccine mandates .

As part of his conservative remake of Florida policies , DeSantis appointed the current surgeon general, Dr. Joseph Ladapo , to the position in 2021. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ladapo emerged as a leading medical freedom advocate and vaccine skeptic.

Ladapo opposes all vaccine mandates . He also proposed new Florida health rules in October 2026 to drop mandates for four vaccines required for school attendance, including chickenpox and hepatitis B. Currently, the state allows exemptions only for approved religious or medical reasons.
The Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics opposes the rule change on public health grounds.

Donalds has long opposed vaccine mandates and says that he did not personally receive a COVID-19 vaccine . He supports Ladapo’s proposed rule change to reduce school vaccination mandates and said during his campaign that he is open to reappointing Ladapo as surgeon general.

The Florida Legislature, however, will limit how far Donalds can push vaccine policy. The Legislature has mandated measles and polio vaccines for all K-12 public school students, so getting rid of that requirement would require a change in the law.

One of the biggest developments in Florida K-12 education in recent years has been the creation of a system of universal vouchers by DeSantis and the Legislature in 2023. This program allows parents of any income level to use US$8,000 in state money on average, based on county of residence , for their children’s private or homeschooling education.

The universal voucher program has created intense pressure on the state budget. It cost an estimated $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2026 . State auditors have identified accountability problems in tracking funds through the system. Public schools have faced declining enrollment , with fewer resources to serve the neediest students they cannot turn away.

Donalds strongly supports the universal voucher program. He has expressed an interest in making Florida “ the model state for school choice ” by allowing parents to choose among private educational providers competing in the marketplace .

His wife, Erika Donalds, is a former Collier County school board member who operates a network of for-profit charter schools and advocates nationally for school choice . Whether the Donaldses will divest from the charter school business during the governor-elect’s term remains to be seen.

Already, the governor-elect has indicated that he might work with the Legislature to change the way the Florida Education Finance Program funds K-12 schools, allowing districts to spend funds with more flexibility.

During his campaign he also proposed a universal scorecard for the voucher program so that parents can compare educational data on student performance across different types of schools. Currently, only public schools must provide this data.

Donalds can also influence state education policy by appointing the seven members of the Board of Education and then recommending a candidate for commissioner of education for that board to elect. The commissioner and state board oversee the Florida Department of Education and programs from kindergarten through postsecondary education.
They board could also implement new eligibility rules for private school vouchers, as the DeSantis administration has done in the past.
During his campaign, Donalds attempted to distance himself from President Donald Trump , whose policies have proven unpopular even in red states such as Florida.

But in his victory speech on the evening of Nov. 3 , Donalds proudly announced that he had received a congratulatory call from the president. “Mr. President,” he said to a cheering crowd, “I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red.”
This story is an update of a story published on Oct. 28, 2026 . Read more of our stories about Florida .
Liv Coleman is affiliated with the Manatee County Democratic Party.

articles.title: Delayed international support has hampered efforts to contain and treat Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo
articles.author:
<name>Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi, Assistant Professor of Healthcare Administration, Fayetteville State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/olayinka-stephen-ilesanmi-2774601"/>
paras: I visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next.

I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist , and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services.

That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners , which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids.

Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading.

More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference.

The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths.
This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus , whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo.
The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns .

The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks , and African institutions are coordinating a continental response . Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably.
Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time.
Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later.
These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders.

International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance . The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million) .

In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort.
But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak.

In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners.

That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further.
According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response.

The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care.

My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect.

That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola . Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools.

The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions.
In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies.

But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict , in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households.

The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety.

There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved . This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak.

Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial , begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine.
The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss.
I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them.
Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi was the past West Africa Regional Program Lead for Africa CDC.

articles.title: Mammograms can do more than detect breast cancer – they also offer important clues on heart health
articles.author:
<name>Matthew Nudy, Assistant Professor of Medicine and Public Health Sciences, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/matthew-nudy-2259153"/>
paras: If you’re a woman over 40, you have no doubt heard your doctor tell you to get a mammogram as part of routine screening for breast cancer . But there’s another reason, too.

A mammogram can show no sign of breast cancer and still reveal something worth discussing with a doctor: calcium deposits in the medium-sized arteries that carry blood to the breast. These calcium deposits may offer a clue to a woman’s future heart health.

I’m a cardiologist who studies cardiovascular health around menopause . My colleagues and I have investigated how mammograms might help identify women who are at increased risk of heart disease and stroke . Artificial intelligence now makes these calcium deposits – called breast arterial calcification , or BAC – easier to measure.

In October 2026, Maryland became the first U.S. state to require mammography centers to notify patients in writing if these calcium deposits are found in their mammograms. Other states may institute similar rules soon. Research shows that these calcium deposits are a robust marker for cardiovascular risk, and I expect its adoption to grow.
Here’s what women need to know about calcium deposits in the breast – and what they should do if their mammogram shows they have them.

Breast arterial calcification is calcium buildup in the walls of medium-sized arteries that carry blood through the breast. On a mammogram image, the calcium deposits appear as parallel white lines tracing those vessels.

This finding is not a sign of breast cancer. And it differs from the fatty and calcified plaque that can narrow arteries supplying the heart muscle. In the case of breast arterial calcification, the calcium lies mainly in the artery’s muscular wall, where it is associated with blood vessel stiffening.

Finding breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not, by itself, establish that a woman has heart disease or a blocked heart artery. But research has now clearly shown that this marker signals that a person’s risk of these outcomes is elevated.
It’s important to remember, however, that its absence does not rule out cardiovascular disease or an increased risk of heart attack or stroke.

Doctors have known about breast arterial calcification for decades, with studies in the 1980s linking it to diabetes and advanced kidney disease . Early findings about its relationship with heart disease were mixed , and many studies were small and relied on radiologists’ visual review of mammograms.

In 2022, my colleagues and I published the results of a 10-year study in which radiologists reviewed mammograms of more than 1,000 women to identify these calcium deposits. Women who had them had about three times the odds of developing coronary heart disease and five times the odds of having a stroke compared with women who didn’t, even after taking age into account.

To confirm that breast arterial calcification in mammograms predicts cardiovascular risk, we assessed 45 published studies involving more than 68,000 women , in a type of study called a meta-analysis . This work, published in 2026, found that women who had these calcium deposits in their breast arteries on a mammogram had roughly twice the risk of stroke, heart failure and death from any cause, and nearly three times the risk of dying from heart disease, compared with women who did not.

The studies we analyzed differed considerably in design and quality, so these averages cannot precisely predict an individual woman’s cardiovascular risk. Also, while these findings establish an association between breast arterial calcification and cardiovascular disease, they do not show that calcium in the breast arteries causes those health outcomes.

Radiologists can see breast artery calcium on a routine mammogram. But there’s no common standard for grading and reporting how much calcification is present. AI tools which are being used more commonly by doctors can measure how much is there using the same images, with no extra radiation.

These calcium deposits become more common with age, so my colleagues and I used AI to assess data from more than 100,000 women in nine countries in order to map how calcium builds up in breast arteries by age. We developed and tested a metric that, when added to standard tools, improved doctors’ ability to accurately predict a woman’s risk of cardiovascular disease.

Maryland became the first state to require a notice about breast arterial calcification in screening results. The goal is to give women who have it a reason to talk with their doctor about heart health.

The bill’s sponsor modeled the law on a 2023 regulation on breast density notices , which required mammography centers to inform patients and their doctors about their breast density and its link to cancer detection. The breast density rule was first implemented in Connecticut and then adopted by many other states, before becoming a nationwide requirement .

An Australian trial called TIM-TAM will test whether using breast arterial calcification to guide care improves measures of heart health. Researchers still need to find out whether treating women based on the presence of breast arterial calcification prevents heart attacks or strokes. But research already shows that the marker has a link to cardiovascular disease, and I expect it to follow a similar pattern of adoption as reporting breast density.

Until other states adjust their requirements, look for “breast arterial calcification” or “vascular calcifications” in the radiologist’s report. Mammography centers’ reporting practices vary, so some reports may omit BAC even when it’s visible. Some imaging centers offer an optional AI review for breast arterial calcification as an out-of-pocket add-on to a screening mammogram.

On its own, the presence of breast arterial calcification on a mammogram does not determine whether someone needs a heart test or a new prescription. But in my view, this marker can provide a useful nudge to get an updated assessment of cardiovascular health.
Your doctor may suggest a blood pressure measurement and blood tests for cholesterol and kidney function. An estimate called eGFR describes how well the kidneys filter blood.

Your doctor can use these results alongside age, smoking, diabetes and other information in the American Heart Association’s PREVENT calculator . It estimates the chance of developing cardiovascular disease over the next 10 years for adults ages 30 to 79 who are not already diagnosed with cardiovascular disease.

You can then discuss with your doctor which steps could make the biggest difference for your heart health depending on your risk. That might mean finding ways to move more, choosing foods that are good for your heart or getting help to quit smoking if you smoke. Depending on your overall risk, your doctor may also suggest taking a statin to lower your cholesterol or starting or adjusting blood pressure medicine. These treatments can help lower your chances of a heart attack or stroke.
A routine breast screening visit can thus become an opportunity to help women understand their cardiovascular risk and take steps to lower it.
Matthew Nudy is supported by the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences, Grant KL2 TR002015 and Grant UL1 TR002014.

articles.title: I research play – and here’s why recess is much more important than just a fun break
articles.author:
<name>Louisa Penfold, Professor of Education, Harvard University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/louisa-penfold-2772627"/>
paras: School recess has long been considered a standard part of children’s education in the United States. But it’s more than just a fun break from sitting at a desk.
Daily recess is necessary for supporting young children and adolescents’ learning, as well as their physical and mental health .

It’s so important that the American Academy of Pediatrics notes that reducing the amount of time set aside for playing, running and exploring in order to fit in more academic work could actually be counterproductive.
But in recent decades many schools have cut back on recess, which many states do not require .

As a scholar who researches childhood play, I have studied and witnessed the benefits of play in children’s lives, including the significant social, emotional and cognitive impacts it has on students’ overall well-being.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that children and adolescents get at least 60 minutes of physical activity per day.
The CDC also defines recess as a “regularly scheduled period in the school day for physical activity and play that is monitored by trained staff or volunteers.”
Recess can look different across various schools – while some kids play outside on play structures or in grassy fields, others might play indoors during inclement weather.
Research also shows, for example, that children living in lower-income communities have fewer opportunities than their peers in higher-income communities to play outside.
Unlike physical education classes or participating in organized sports, recess gives students the time to engage in physical activity and interact with their peers however they like.

This time for unstructured play can offer much-needed relief from the mental focus that students need to maintain throughout the school day. It can also support their cognitive development and overall emotional and physical well-being.
Research also consistently shows that giving children breaks each day for recess has immense benefits for their mental health and the executive functioning skills that support academic achievement.
This includes benefits for students’ focus and creativity , as well as their memory and executive function .
Most states do not mandate that schools have recess every day or spell out a minimum amount of time students must spend moving their bodies.

A 2025 report from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health found that 11 states have laws addressing school recess. This ranges from Arizona’s requirement for 40 minutes of daily recess to Georgia, Indiana and Kentucky all requiring recess, but with no minimum duration.

Massachusetts is one of the nearly 40 states without any laws regarding recess time. A recent article in The Boston Globe reported schools in Cambridge having 25 minutes of recess, while other schools across the state had only 15 minutes per day.

Overall, there has been an uptick in state legislation aimed at preserving mandated daily school recess time, thanks partly to a new parent-led advocacy group called Say Yes to Recess . This group is pushing for schools across the country to provide a minimum of 60 minutes of protected school recess time each day.
Started by three Tennessee moms, Say Yes to Recess has also helped advocate for Tennessee legislation that increased the state’s mandated daily school recess time from 15 to 40 minutes in July 2025.
During the 2001-02 school year, elementary school students from 349 school districts spent on average 36.8 minutes per day at recess.
By 2025, the CDC found that students were spending 27 minutes on average in recess each day.
It’s also hard to track how much physical activity students get at school because public school districts and private schools often do not record and report this information.

While the benefits of recess are not just isolated to young children , a 2026 international study showed that the amount of daily recess time across U.S. schools declines from a mean of 39.3 minutes per day for 6- to 7-year-olds to 24.5 minutes per day for 12- to 18-year-olds.
I conducted research at the Project Zero research center for creativity, ethics and the arts at Harvard University and highlighted the significance of play and the arts within urban public schools.

This 2024 study showed how play with materials supports both children’s and teachers’ creative learning. As someone who designs and studies children’s play spaces, I worry about what could happen if schools continue to reduce school recess because of staffing issues, budget cuts or prioritization of students’ preparation for high-stakes tests focused solely on literacy and numeracy.
Research shows that this trend of not prioritizing recess could have significant effects on children’s and adolescents’ mental health, cognitive development and overall enjoyment of school.

The decline in time for recess comes at a moment when many schools and districts are under increasing pressure as a result of declining student enrollment , pressure to meet state learning standards and budget cuts .
For some schools, reduced staffing and the costs of maintaining outdoor play equipment to meet safety requirements have made it difficult to offer school recess.
For other schools, an assumption that more time for instruction equals a higher-quality education may be driving decisions to minimize or eliminate time for unstructured play.
Another factor that influences recess is when schools deny students recess time as a form of punishment – a policy that some scholars and educators are trying to block through legislation .

As childhood health, social and cognitive research demonstrates, the amount of time school recess is given matters in children’s development as whole human beings. I believe it is up to schools, districts and parents to advocate for and ensure children’s right to protected school recess time every day.
Harvard Graduate School of Education Project Zero at the Harvard Graduate School of Education

articles.title: Why do blind people and musicians hear pitch better? New research suggests they have less internal noise
articles.author:
<name>Woon Ju Park, Assistant Professor of Psychology, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/woon-ju-park-1494279"/>
paras: People who have lived most of their lives blind often have extraordinary hearing abilities . In new research published in the Journal of Neuroscience, my colleagues and I discovered that this ability arises from how their auditory systems are able to more consistently and reliably process sounds compared with people who aren’t blind. And interestingly, sighted musicians seem to enhance their hearing through a similar mechanism.
Hearing is a complicated process. It involves many stages , starting from how the ears detect sounds and going all the way up to how the brain extracts meaningful information from those sounds.

Different mechanisms are involved, too. You can get better at hearing by being more selective or more consistent . Think of writing the letter “A.” You can practice to make your “A” either more distinguishable from “B” or look more similar to other “A’s” every time you write it. The latter is called internal noise – how consistently your auditory system responds to the same sound over time. The less internal noise you have, the more reliably you can tell similar sounds apart.

We recruited nine individuals who became blind before the age of 2 and 18 sighted individuals. Participants in both groups had varying levels of musical training, giving us an opportunity to examine how musical experience can also affect hearing abilities.

Participants completed two simple hearing tasks. In one task, they detected a tone presented in background noise, which allowed us to assess how the cochlea in the inner ear processes different sound frequencies. In the other task, they judged which of the two tones had a higher pitch, a task that also relies on how the brain interprets sound information.

We found that people with early-life blindness were better than sighted people only in the pitch discrimination task. This means that their improved hearing abilities may selectively originate from changes in how their brains process auditory information and not from how their ears detect sounds.

Importantly, we used a mathematical model to better understand what drives differences in pitch discrimination. The model showed that the enhanced ability to tell pitches apart in people with early-life blindness happens by reducing internal noise : more consistent and reliable processing of sounds rather than greater selectivity for different sound frequencies.

Surprisingly, we found that musical training seems to similarly reduce internal noise. Sighted musicians also responded to sounds more consistently compared with people who neither experienced early-life blindness nor received extensive musical training.
Because your brain doesn’t know what kind of sensory environment it’ll encounter when you’re born, it’s equipped with a special ability: to tune its responses to parts of the world that matter to it.

This ability helps people see, hear and master new skills as their experiences change, like when children learn to read and when adults learn to identify different bird species . Words and birds have become a meaningful part of their experiences, so their brains are tuned to the new information.

Our study identifies internal noise as an important factor that facilitates this brain plasticity . There are many ways a person can come to have reduced levels of internal noise, and one is by building a more accurate template for perceiving the world.
It is possible that sensory experience, whether it be being blind or being a musician, might help create and fine-tune the perceptual template relevant for hearing.

If sensory experiences and training can tap into the brain’s ability to adapt, researchers may be able to use them to improve perceptual abilities. For example, targeted training to hear sound locations could help people who are beginning to lose vision learn to rely on other senses to navigate.
However, researchers still don’t know how much training is needed and what aspects of the auditory experience are key to drive behaviorally meaningful changes in the brain.

Another important question is whether and how this brain plasticity varies depending on when someone loses their vision or begins musical training. The brain might have greater plasticity early in development, and how sensory experiences shape the brain may differ in adulthood.

How far can people push their ability to learn? Can everyone become super listeners with training? If the brain’s plasticity is limited in adulthood, are there ways to reopen the door? And what role does internal noise play in this learning?

Moving forward, our team is interested in understanding whether the enhanced pitch discrimination we saw in people with early-life blindness and sighted musicians extends to more complex, everyday listening.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

articles.title: Democrats on Course for Supermajority in Washington State House, Election Night Results Show
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Democrats scored victories up and down the ballot across the country Tuesday night, and the picture in Washington state was no different. Election night returns, when about half of ballots are counted in Washington's vote-by-mail elections, indicated Democrats are likely on course to a two-thirds supermajority in the state House.

The Urbanist laid out the path to a Democratic supermajority in our post-primary analysis , and basically everything that could break their way did. Legislative District 17 and 18 in Clark County swung from Republicans to Democrats, as did LD14 in the Yakima Valley, clearing indicating a shift among Latino voters and high turnout in the Democratic base.

The last Republican holdout in Kitsap County's Legislative District 26 is no more, giving Democrats another pickup. Urbanist-endorsed Democrat Renee Hernandez Greenfield is up nearly 10 points over Republican Katy Cornell, who was hoping to pick up the baton from retiring Rep. Michelle Caldier.

The Democratic gains build on a decade of steady progress expanding their legislative margins. After the 2024 election, Democrats surpassed 60% in both chambers, but most supermajority advantages, like the possibility of passing amendments to the state constitution, kick in at the two-thirds mark.

Even races not fully on the radar as realistic pickup opportunities, like LD12 Position 1 and the LD35 senate race saw Democrats in the lead on election night. These largely rural districts have long been Republican strongholds.

In the 25th LD, school board director David Berg is leading Republican Rep. Michael Keaton by 1.6 points. The 25th represents the last district in the Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area still held by Republicans after a decade of steady losses. Republican seatmate Cyndy Jacobsen is grasping to a razor-thin 109-vote lead over Democratic challenger Jenn Marie Strickling.

In the 35th, Democrat Carolina Mejia has a three-point lead over incumbent Republican Drew MacEwan. Down ballot, the Republican incumbents Dan Griffey and Travis Couture hold slim leads under one point. Democrat Jim Pierson is just 212 votes behind Griffey with tons of votes still to count.

In the 12th, Democrat challenger Stacy Willoughby is up three points over incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Burnett. The district covers Chelan County and crosses the Cascades into the eastern reaches of King and Snohomish counties. Republican seatmate Rep. Mike Steele is comfortably ahead, meanwhile, suggesting Burnett's profile – a Trump-endorsed former Chelan County sheriff is particularly odious to voters right now.

In the 39th, Republicans are also clinging to thin leads. On election night, Democrat Ida Keeley trailed Republican Steve Ewing by just 282 votes, with both vying to replace Rep. Caroline Eslick, who retired. GOP incumbent Sam Low had a larger five-point lead over Democrat Kathryn Lewandowsky in the Position 1 race. In 2024, a Democrat didn't even make it though the primary to face Low, and no Democrat ran against Eslick at all.

While likely on the path to a two-thirds majority in the state House, Democrats were not able to make quite the same gains in the state Senate, where only half of the seats are up in any given year. In a stroke of bad luck for Democrats, several Republican-held seats in more swing-y districts were not up this year, including LD14, LD17, LD25, and LD39. However, it could be tough sledding for those Republican incumbents in 2028 unless the state's political mood shifts significantly.

If election night leads hold, the Democrats' advantage in the state house will grow from 59-39 to 66-32, just across the two-thirds threshold. Pulling ahead in some or all of the close races in LD25-2, LD35-1, LD35-2, and LD39-2 would expand that supermajority.
Some efforts from conservative megadonors to defend centrist Democrats from progressive challenges also fell flat.

In the 48th LD, Redmond Councilmember Jessica Forsythe (who is Urbanist-endorsed) is leading incumbent State Rep. Amy Walen by five points in election night results, despite more than a $1 million in outside spending. Microsoft-funded Washington Need to Compete political action committee (PAC) led the way investing $700,000 in the race. Walen once one of the few Democrats to vote against the millionaires tax, drawing ire from the progressive wing of the party. Forsythe saw a fair share of spending on her own behalf, with the state-employee funded New Direction PAC putting up more than $300,000 against Walen on top of $260,000 to promote Forsythe.

In the 29th LD, Democratic Rep. Melanie Morgan looks like she will lose to progressive, Urbanist-endorser challenger Krista Perez, after trailing by three points on election night. Morgan voted against the millionaires tax, breaking with her caucus.

Republicans also launched a frontal assault on the millionaires tax via statewide Initiative Measure No. 645, aiming to repeal the tax and blow a major hole in the state budget. That measure was resoundingly defeated, falling just short of 42% of the vote on election night. Democrats seeking to triangulate in opposing the millionaires tax seem to have made a miscalculation; they would have been more popular if they voted for it.

Republican efforts to force conservative judges onto the state Supreme Court also appears to have fizzled. The one exception is that Ian Birk (Urbanist-endorsed) is trailing Republican-backed Sean O'Donnell by two points, and will need to close the gap in later returns to survive. A Supreme Court takeover would have offered another route for conservatives to block the millionaires tax or other similar progressive revenue sources, but it doesn't look like the scheme worked.

Let's Go Washington, a PAC led by hedge fund multimillionaire Brian Heywood, ran the repeal measure along with two initiatives targeting trans rights . Initiative Measure 1 (which forces schools to potentially out queer kids to unsupportive parents) looks like it will fail, as it's down five points. However, Initiative Measure 638, which seeks to block trans girls from participating in school athletics, looks like it will pass, as it has 56% of the vote so far.
The setback on trans rights was one of the few blemishes on an otherwise triumphant night for progressives.
Correction : The initial version of this article incorrectly listed Amy Walen as a state senator, rather than a state representative.

articles.title: Transit Measures Headed to Victory in Seattle, Pierce County
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Bus riders in Seattle and Pierce County are poised to see increased transit service in the wake of successful funding measures, with early returns showing strong voter support in both jurisdictions. Seattle's transit measure, which renews an existing sales tax measure supplementing King County Metro service, is ahead with 72.5% of the vote, while the funding measure for Pierce Transit is leading with a very respectable 57.7%.

Both propositions will bump up the local sales tax rate by 0.3% to fund bus service, with Seattle's measure set to enable nearly 100,000 more King County Metro bus trips every year on top of the 180,000 currently provided. It would also continue funding existing transit-related programs, including streetcar service and a major expansion of the number of subsidized ORCA transit cards provided by the City of Seattle.

Pierce Transit's measure will bump up service by nearly 50% compared to the levels seen today, expanding hours of operation and frequency across the entire network along with adding four brand new bus routes. It will also enable the agency to eliminate fares for seniors, building on the existing statewide free youth fare program.

A success at the ballot box in Seattle was all but assured, given the track record of the existing Seattle Transit Measure, which has been in place since 2014. The 2020 renewal passed with 80.3% of the vote , a nationwide record for a transit funding measure that has still never been surpassed. But for Pierce Transit, things were much less less certain in terms of going to the voters for more funding.

Serving Tacoma, Puyallup, Lakewood, University Place, Spanaway and Gig Harbor, Pierce Transit has been operating at a lower funding level than other peer agencies across the region for decades. A pair of defeated measures in 2011 and 2012 led to substantial service cuts and a contraction of the agency's total service area.
Those defeats ultimately led to a reluctance to head back to the ballot that was overcome this year, prompted by strong polling and high expected turnout during a midterm election.

The results are a major source of vindication for Pierce County's elected transit champions, including Tacoma City Councilmember Kristina Walker and Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello. Mello has been clear about the need to expand transit access in Pierce County since being elected in 2024, taking over after eight years of Republican leadership.

"For me, what it means is finally having a transit system that will connect more people to opportunity, to run their life and the essentials of their life," Mello told The Urbanist in an interview Wednesday morning. "So many of the things that I'm working on: connecting people to opportunity, connecting people to jobs, getting to school, after school programs to keep people safe, connecting vulnerable community members to healthcare and other services — the common barrier, time and time again, is transportation."

The 47% increase in service will be phased in by the early 2030s, ending the era of the hourly bus on the Pierce Transit network. The number of bus routes that operate every 30 minutes will jump from 18 to 24, with seven routes going to 15-20 minutes – frequency boosts that will represent a game changer for access across Pierce County.
Mello told The Urbanist that the 15-point margin on election night was a pleasant surprise.

"I was prepared for a much closer margin. I know we ran a really good campaign. I know we had a really clear message about what we were going to deliver, but you know, it's a tax measure in this economy, in this significant sense of uncertainty, there was a lot of concern about: would voters still be willing to invest in themselves and our community in this way," Mello said. "But they they surely see the value of making sure that more people can get access to opportunity, and I'm so proud of my neighbors for seeing the power of transit to connect more people to opportunity."

The passage of the Seattle Transit Measure Tuesday night notches a major win for Mayor Katie Wilson, who proposed doubling the existing 0.15% sales tax rate to 0.3%. Though that move was met with a hand-wringing over cost impacts that hasn't been seen with other sales tax bumps – including a 0.1% increase for public safety investments approved last year by her predecessor Bruce Harrell – Wilson made the case that increasing access to transit will outweigh the sales tax bump when it comes to the affordability impact for city residents.

"I just want to drive home the point that this is an affordability measure, and when gas is $6 a gallon, when the price of car ownership has never been higher, this measure – fast, frequent bus service, is going to allow more people, more households around our city, to get around on a most affordable mode of transportation," Wilson told transit supporters gathered at a Proposition 1 party in Pioneer Square. "And we are not going to stop until Seattle's transit system is irresistibly good."

Wilson was clearly in her element Tuesday night, with the win representing a full circle moment. Prior to being elected Mayor, Wilson led the Transit Riders Union, an organization that got its start advocating for transit funding in Seattle. In 2011, Wilson helped to launch the Save Our Metro! campaign to push against pending Metro service cuts stemming from the Great Recession. After those cuts were averted with a $20 car tab fee approved by the King County Council, the group pivoted to other transit fights including a push for a countywide low-income fare program.

"Seattle is not just a great transit city; it is the great transit city. And tonight shows us that that is still true," Wilson said. "This year has been a banner year for public transit in our city and our region. We've had some of the highest rebounding ridership in the country. We have opened up some of the most ambitious capital infrastructure anywhere in the U.S. We now have a light rail station that has the highest ridership of any light rail system in the whole entire country."
With the 2 Line now crossing Lake Washington, Sound Transit has surpassed 160,000 daily boardings, making it the most-ridden light rail system in the country.

With Seattle largely maxing out its transit funding capabilities with this renewal, attention is set to turn to King County Metro, which will be buoyed by this funding but still in need of a more sustainable long-term funding source to keep the agency stable. The millionaire's tax voters also upheld Tuesday means even less sales tax funding will be flowing into Metro's coffers at the end of this decade than had been expected, due to planned sales tax exemptions. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay will have to start to address a looming budget shortfall by next year's biennial budget.

"Seattle and King County residents deserve safe, affordable, and world-class transit. Renewing the Seattle Transit Measure reflects voters’ commitment to stronger, more connected communities by adding thousands of hours of Metro service, expanding early morning and late-night service, and providing free transit passes to more students, working families, and low-income residents," Zahilay said in a statement after the results dropped. "This historic investment will help Metro reach more communities and ensure more people have a sustainable, affordable, reliable way to get where they need to go."

The transit funding push across the region isn't even over. On Wednesday night, the Everett City Council will decide whether to give the green light for Community Transit to annex Everett Transit , trading away the city-specific 0.6% sales tax rate for Community Transit's 1.2%. That move will come with a 50% increase in transit service within the city by 2031, and transit connections that simply can't exist with Snohomish County's largest city maintaining a completely separate transit agency.
Wednesday's vote will be followed by a vote of the Community Transit board on Thursday.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law, Everett Transit's annexation will be able to happen without the voters directly weighing in. But the move represents a bold swing by three-term Everett Mayor Cassie Franklin, who has been making the case that the city can't grow sustainably without making substantial investments in transit.

Earlier this year, voters in and around Spokane also signed onto a 0.2% sales tax measure that will allow Spokane Transit to maintain existing service and grow in the future. Clearly, the momentum is on the side of transit expansion in 2026 in Washington State.

articles.title: Why a Seattle Electric Vehicle Charging Lot Is Taking Half a Decade to Build
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: How long does it take to build eight parking stalls? For Seattle City Light, the answer to that question remains a moving target.

Since 2022, Seattle City Light (SCL) has been trying to build a surface parking lot for electric vehicle charging in West Seattle's Morgan Junction neighborhood, on a former substation that had been sitting decommissioned for 20 years. The 4,500-square-foot site is set to see eight paid, fast-charging stations, which City Light touts as bringing EV charging "closer to neighborhood retail, services, and major arterial roads in Morgan Junction." But the project has faced numerous setbacks, with the publicly owned utility recently firing its contractor in the middle of construction.

Even in a city where timelines for public works projects often stretch longer than originally promised, the Morgan Junction charging lot has become a symbol of frustration with local government being able to deliver on promises. When the project was launched in 2022, City Light noted that construction could begin as soon as that year, and take approximately three months. Now, the lot doesn't look poised to open until September of 2027.

The West Seattle Blog has studiously chronicled the long saga of the Morgan Junction charging lot over its years of planning and development, either directly or by covering updates at monthly meetings of the Morgan Community Association. That reporting has shown timelines that continued to slip as the project advanced through design, even before being beset by issues during construction.

"Morgan Junction is our largest and most ambitious EV-charging station project to date requiring more time, engineering, and permitting than one of our more typical EV charging station projects," a former SCL spokesperson told the WSB in late 2024 , when the lot was still in design. "We’ve also experienced significant delays with procurement of the chargers and other electric service equipment. This is likely due to the rapid increase in transportation electrification costs nationwide."

In early 2025, District 1 Councilmember Rob Saka announced that his office had taken "decisive steps" to "accelerate the timeline" for the project, publishing an internal SCL memo laying out a schedule that would allow the city to start construction that October. But it wasn't until February of this year that contractor Zenisco Inc. did actually start work.

Five months later, construction work was halted on the site after the city found an issue: the east wall of the site needed a redesign due to work-quality issues and site conditions, in order to maintain the barrier between the lot and the adjacent alleyway.

"While crews worked on site during the FIFA construction moratorium, City Light construction engineers identified a significant structural design issue," SCL said in an update to the West Seattle Blog in July . "This required a complete work stoppage and will further delay the project so the project team can develop a solution. We will provide an estimated completion date for the charging station once the solution is approved by permitting authorities."
Just a few weeks later, after the design issue was resolved, SCL fired Zenisco, a decision that looked to stem from those aforementioned site quality issues.

"This project has taken longer than we planned, and we understand the frustration that comes with that. We’re committed to completing this work and opening the station for the Morgan Junction and all who visit," SCL posted in an update to the project website in September.

As of that time, the City was still waiting on next steps when it came to securing a new contractor, but did set the new completion date of September of 2027. Another schedule slip likely wouldn't shock anyone following this project, however.

The Morgan Junction site is far from the only site where City Light has run into issues implementing a standalone EV charging lot. In 2021, SCL proposed to convert another decommissioned substation along NW Market Street in Ballard to a charging lot, but backed off after doing early planning work.

"A soil test determined that on-site drainage options would not work and the only viable drainage option was to install a connection to the municipal stormwater sewer on the south side of NW Market Street," a 2022 SCL update on that project stated. "Seattle City Light decided that the added cost and disruption to vehicle traffic and King County Metro trolley bus operations on NW Market Street made this project unviable. Seattle City Light may resume work if a less disruptive method of providing site drainage is found."

After abandoning that project, SCL turned its attention to a site in Belltown , a leftover parcel owned by the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). Originally eyed as a spot for a potential public playground as part of the Waterfront Park redevelopment, a potential land swap for a nearby SCL property on the future site of Portal Park opened up the opportunity for EV charging.

In the face of significant concerns about using such a high-value site near Pike Place Market as another surface parking lot, SCL abandoned that project as well, citing "unforeseen delays and funding constraints."
For now, City Light appears to be pivoting away from the idea of building more standalone lots, according to SCL spokesperson Kate Jacobs.
"Our planned expansion does not include comparable sites that would require new lots," Jacobs wrote via email.

The utility has had much more success in adding curbside charging in the public right-of-way, aiming for 200 on-street charging locations by 2030 via funding from the 2024 Seattle Transportation levy.
And as for the Morgan Junction lot, where work is expected to soon resume? Jacobs said that SCL will be learning from its stumbles there as soon as the ribbon is cut.

"We will conduct a comprehensive review of all phases of the project as soon as we’ve delivered this important asset to the community," Jacobs wrote. "Implementing lessons learned is part of our standard process, and lessons from Morgan Junction and past projects will improve how we deliver public charging as we expand our network to meet growing demand."

articles.title: Conservatives Take Their Swings as 2026 Election Trends Toward Progressives
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Right-wing extremism had been having a moment, but tonight's election could be a major setback against that push and a leftward shift for the United States – at least if polling is on the mark. While polls have been positive for Democrats, right-wing leaders are not taking this lying down. In fact, the wealthy elite are spending at unprecedented levels.

Elon Musk alone has poured nearly a half billion dollars into the midterm elections, hoping to keep Republicans in power and hold back a blue wave. As the world's richest person, Musk obviously has an interest in continuing Trump tax cuts, shielding his personal and corporate wealth and lining up further political favors for his companies.

Some of Washington state's wealthiest people are also looking to influence elections in a big way. Hedge fund manager Brian Heywood is leading the way with his three statewide initiatives that will strip rights from queer students, require genital inspections for female athletes, and block the state's new millionaires tax, which is set to go into effect in 2029.

With Washington voters increasingly backing Democrats and giving them a strong trifecta in Olympia, uberwealthy conservatives increasingly are getting creative in their attempts to control political outcomes, spending millions on signature gathering efforts to force initiatives onto the ballot to repeal laws or pass new ones. Beyond the statewide measures, Heywood and his conservative cronies are looking to restructure Snohomish County government to make it easy for conservatives to veto progress, even when in a legislative minority.

Corporate elites are getting into the act, too. Microsoft and other top companies put together a Washington Need to Compete political action committee (PAC) with a huge war chest. So far, the PAC has run an ad criticizing the direction in Olympia during two primetime Seahawks football games. Washington Observer 's Paul Query reported that Washington Need to Compete has amassed $14 million, but has spent only $3 million, keeping most in reserve for 2027.

"[The ads are] intended as a warning shot to the Legislature and Gov. Bob Ferguson, and it seems to have pissed the latter right off," Query wrote. "Last week, at the Seattle Chamber’s Regional Leadership Conference, a schmoozy affair held out at the Suncadia resort, Ferguson teed off on the Redmond-based software behemoth."
The ad struck a nerve, with Ferguson bringing up that the state was smashing records for venture capital investment in startups.

"If we're partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right," Ferguson said in the recording. "If I ran some multi-million-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft for some things, you guys all would think I've lost my mind."

Ferguson continued to extend an olive branch, even as he questioned the communication style Microsoft and friends were using. He also cast doubt on the threat they appeared to be trying to deliver that they could dislodge him with big campaign spending to propel a political challenger from the right, adding he planned on being governor for a "long time."

"Washington State sure as heck as a government can do more and do better by all of you folks and all the workers you represent, but it works both ways, right?" Ferguson told the chamber crowd. "It works both ways, and so that's what I would say: I plan on being governor for a long time. I work with all of you, Microsoft included, who I work well with. But I do have some questions about how we communicate."

Microsoft targeting Ferguson is a bit surprising since he's operated as a centrist and taken pains to push for budget cuts over new taxes. Even though Ferguson ultimately signed the millionaires tax , he quickly pivoted to saying it was time for budget cuts after setting the new tax in motion, which will take several years to bring in revenue given its long implementation runway.

The millionaires tax clearly is high on the list of policy changes angering the corporate establishment. One of the legislative races that the Microsoft-funded PAC has spent most heavily is the state senate race in the 48th Legislative District, where more union-backed, left-leaning Redmond Mayor Jessica Forsythe is seeking to unseat State Rep. Amy Walen, who was one of the few votes against the millionaires tax in the Democratic caucus. The PAC has spent more than $700,000 defending her. Clearly, the ultrarich do not want to see Walen go.

While millionaires worry about slightly higher tax bills, many Americans have growing concerns about covering basic necessities and making ends meet as Trump's war in Iran drags on, driving up fuel prices. Trump's tariff regime is also driving up consumer prices, taking money out of families' pockets while alienating allied nations.

Health care workers and advocates under the banner of the Healthcare and Human Rights Coalition held a rally in Renton last week to demand universal health care. A chorus of speakers made the case, noting that Trump's actions were driving up health care costs for many Americans by kicking people off Medicaid and disrupting insurance marketplaces that had moderated costs.

King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda, who is up for reelection and is endorsed by The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve), spoke at the rally, saying a crisis also brings opportunity.

"Now is the time for action. Don't waste a crisis," Mosqueda said. "We know that other countries with similar GDP, similar economies, similar capitalist mentalities have already committed to healthcare as a human right, and that's why we're demanding universal healthcare for all. And we're not here to wait for the cavalry to come from the feds. We're not here to wait to make sure that the D.C. folks can hear us and take action to repeal H.R. 1. We're here to call for action right here in Washington State, right here in King County."

Speakers decried work requirements that Trump added to Medicaid as part of H.R. 1, which could lead to millions more being uninsured and without health care access. In addition to harming those in poverty, health care policy changes also put women and trans people at risk.

Jaelynn Scott, who is running unopposed for the state House in the 37th Legislative District, with The Urbanist's endorsement . Scott is executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a national Black trans feminist organization advancing justice for gender diverse communities, and noted a proxy way was going on targeting the bodies of LGBTQ people.

"I want to [give a] thank you to the Healthcare and Human Rights Coalition for organizing this gathering as we watch the Trump administration give billionaires tax cuts and pass through costs to our state," Scott said. "We're sitting aside and waiting on action from our state legislature. Look, the billionaires and Trump administration are playing proxy wars on our bodies. Nowhere, nowhere is that more evident than with the communities that I organize with – that's LGBTQ communities, the communities that I'm running to represent in the 37th."
Scott alluded to Republican increasing attacks on trans people as a means to fire up their base despite failures and broken promises on other issues.

"They are attacking specifically trans communities and stripping our health care," Scott said. "So, now we're in the position as a state that we have to do Medicaid backfill, and we're going to do the bare minimum. But we have to do more than the bare minimum. How can we ensure that we show that Washington State is a state that actually is a sanctuary for all, and that healthcare is a human right, and that gender-affirming care is great in this state?"

If Democrats succeed nationally in retaking Congress, repealing H.R. 1 would be a bold goal, but one within their reach. Barring action, health care will become increasingly unaffordable for working families and some will lack access altogether.
Correction : The initial version of this article incorrectly listed Amy Walen as a state senator, rather than a state representative.

articles.title: County adjusts Broadway crisis center construction budget to $35M as facility plans take shape
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: King County Public Health is addressing rising cost projections for its planned Central Crisis Care Center on Broadway, telling CHS that a newly proposed $35 million budget request reflects refined project requirements, not cost overrun.

The county acquired the former Polyclinic building at 1110 Harvard Ave for $41.5 million to create a 24/7 walk-in behavioral health facility. An early renovation estimate of $16 to 17 million in early discussions around the project was a preliminary “Rough Order of Magnitude” figure, according to a spokesperson.

That initial projection accounted only for hard construction expenses, omitting soft costs such as engineering, architectural design, permitting, and owner contingencies before operational programming with designated operator Connections Health Solutions had begun.

To keep the redevelopment on track for a targeted late-2027 opening, the County Facilities Management Division has requested a $35 million authorization, funded by rebalancing the voter-approved Crisis Care Centers Levy implementation budget.
Final construction figures and schematic designs will be released once a general contractor joins the team early next year, the spokesperson said.

Officials also confirmed that the property’s vacant southern lot will be addressed. After building renovations are fully designed, the county will consult neighbors and the City of Seattle on potential uses, including community-requested green space.

CHS reported here last month on the beginning of a key land use review process for the facility for interior and exterior upgrades that “apply the principles of trauma-informed design, and recognize the unique needs of individuals across the lifespan” at the medical building on the edge between First Hill and Capitol Hill.
The new construction outlook would push the total price tag on the project above $76 million for the acquisition and transformation of the three-story building.

A citizen-led Seattle Community Advisory Group formed to help shape planning for the project is also working to allocate an additional $3 million county mitigation fund to address street disorder and public safety gaps.
CHS reported on the advisory group’s early work around public safety improvements focused heavily on surrounding street conditions.

articles.title: Pop Loser: Chastity Belt’s New Album Made Me Cry
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: Welcome back to Pop Loser! This week I’ll dive into Chastity Belt’s new album All My Friends (out Friday on Suicide Squeeze), the best musician costumes I saw this Halloween, and that time the Pet Shop Boys produced an album for Liza Minnelli. There are so many great shows happening in Seattle this week, and I’m overwhelmed. Plus, do you remember where you were when Justin Timberlake unveiled Janet Jackson’s semi-shielded nipple?

This week in Strangerland, I interviewed Corin Tucker about reviving her first band, Heavens to Betsy (don’t miss their show with Nudity at Neumos tomorrow!). Jullianne Bell reviewed Beabadoobee ’s Halloween-themed concert at Climate Pledge Arena. And in her column, Dear Hendrix , Eva Walker wrote about being an American goth.

Our November print issue has hit the stands, which means there’s a new calendar of music events that’ll keep you busy all month long. I also profiled the best band you haven’t heard (yet), XOË , who is stopping by the Stranger office for Noise Complaint this Friday . Plus, Dave Segal has a fresh batch of new music you shouldn’t miss .

I’m overwhelmed! Too many great shows are happening this week, and I don’t know how to manage my time. Jody Stephens, the last surviving member of the greatest band ever, Big Star, is playing at the Neptune tonight as Big Star Quartet . Seattle’s own instrumental psych rock trio, Iroiro , is playing a record release show on Thursday with Mt Fog and Ononos. On Saturday, mary in the junkyard is playing Barboza, and Big Freedia is playing a tiny show at Substation on Sunday (I’m baffled that it hasn’t sold out yet). The real dilemma comes on Tuesday, though, when Ms. Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean are celebrating 30 years of The Score on the same night as L7 , Syd , and Tiny Vipers . Ahhh!

Chastity Belt’s new album, All My Friends , is out this Friday. Written across multiple years and time zones, the Seattle-based band’s sixth album reflects the thing that’s been their guiding light: friendship. “A lot of times in life I feel like a late bloomer, like I’m still trying to get my shit together in a way that other people have already figured out,” says drummer/vocalist Gretchen Grimm. “But then I reflect on my adulthood, and my top priority has largely been my friends, which I do not regret at all.” Upon my first listen to the album, the lyric “Sewing machine and reality TV / Sleepovers at 34” (“Friends For This”) made me shed a literal tear of joy. My love for Chastity Belt started hand in hand with my own best and oldest friend, Myka. Back in the summer of 2013, we would drive around Alki Beach in her VW Cabriolet, scheming for beers, complaining about boys, and shouting every word to their debut album No Regerts. All My Friends feels like an ode to the memories that the band’s 15+ year legacy has fostered, both for the band members themselves and for their listeners.

In the words of Phoebe Bridgers, “Baby, it’s Halloween, and we can be anything.” Lily Allen dressed up as an empty Ticketmaster map. Tinashe was a bottle of melatonin. Charli xcx showed up as Secretary ’s smoldering Lee Holloway. Madonna sported a high-concept costume inspired by Jean Cocteau. Sam Smith channeled my favorite era of Liza Minnelli (more on that later), Caroline Polachek dressed as a piano, and Bridgers shared three group costumes from week seven of the Lost Tour, including her band dressed as the cast of Twin Peaks , Peter Pan , and The Wizard of Oz .

A tell-all docuseries about the 2004 Super Bowl incident is coming. Where were you when Justin Timberlake revealed Janet Jackson’s infamous sunburst-shaped nipple shield during the infamous halftime show? I was playing with Polly Pockets in the basement of my friend’s house while her teenage brother watched the game on a mammoth big-screen TV. When the incident happened, he bolted to the VHS player to make sure that it was recording so that he could watch it again. It turned out not to be recording—he was devastated. Now, twelve years later, we are finally getting answers as to how this happened: Timberlake and Jackson are reportedly participating in a new four-part documentary on Apple TV about the fiasco.
Now, take a deep breath and enjoy… Bob Dylan meeting Pope Leo in a hoodie. It’s too bad this happened after Halloween, because it would have made an amazing couple’s costume.

Back in 1989, Liza Minnelli dropped Results , produced (and largely written by) the Pet Shop Boys. The album was the result of her wanting to record a pop album and being a big fan of the synth-pop duo’s hit “Rent.” With its catchy-as-hell songs and ethereal production, the album is slowly becoming one of my most listened-to of the year. (I’m only 37 years too late!) Put “So Sorry, I Said” on a mixtape with Virna Lindt’s “ Underwater Boy ” and Judie Tzuke’s “ Shoot from the Heart .”
