articles.title: Idaho Voters Picked the Evilest Possible State Gun
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Despite the best efforts of the Idaho Republican Party, the state’s people still have the right to propose citizen initiatives, which appear on the ballot alongside initiatives referred by the far-right state Legislature. For instance, Idaho residents this year voted down a grassroots attempt to restore abortion access, as well as a ploy by the Legislature to forever curb marijuana legalization by giving the legislature sole power over the matter.

Those are issues that actually matter which will be dissected by politicos in the weeks and months to come. But I want to talk about the stupidest thing on the Idaho ballot: House Bill 932, which the Legislature placed on the ballot to give We the People the opportunity to choose which firearm should be the official state gun of Idaho.

At the very least we can be happy that Idaho legislators picked six old boomer firearms made of wood and heavy steel rather than some gross modern plastic AR-15 or Glock facsimile (maybe a 3D-printed ghost gun would best reflect Idaho politics, or a Nazi Luger).

These are all proud made-in-America chud guns. The 1894 Winchester’s innovative smokeless cartridges made it great for putting down labor actions in the Pacific Northwest, including the left-wing mining union uprisings that state and federal forces suppressed in 1890s North Idaho multiple times with another new military innovation: concentration camps .

The 1873 Winchester is described on the ballot as “the gun that won the West,” a euphemistic whitewash for our long genocide of the Indigenous peoples beyond the Mississippi (if you ever want to feel really cynical, look up what the Union Army was doing in the Pacific Northwest during the Civil War). The Single Action Army revolver carries much the same reputation, while the Remington 700 is a deer hunting rifle so beloved by outdoorsmen that the US military has used them to snipe people across the globe for decades.

Speaking of sniping, in the grand tradition of pointless leftwing infighting, I must critique the rationale of the South Idaho branch of the Democratic Socialists of America for its endorsement of the Colt 1911 for its supposed anti-fascist merits as the sidearm of choice of American troops in World War II.

While South Idaho DSA is correct that the 1911 was a “weapon against fascism” in WWII, it was also a tool of futile butchery in World War I and related American imperial misadventures, such as our efforts to snuff out the Mexican Revolution. Their assessment of the year 1911 being “the year that the first socialist was elected in Idaho” would also be news to those 1890s radical miners whose elected Populist Party local government was overthrown by the US military. As anyone in North Idaho will tell you, the city slickers down in Boise are always a little out of touch with Panhandle politics, socialists included.

Pound for pound the M1 Garand rifle did more to liberate North Africa and Western Europe from Axis fascism than the humble 1911, but it placed dead last in Idaho’s election (behind the 1911). A reflection of Idaho’s far-right politics? The stakes are low enough that it’s a conclusion I’m willing to jump to. The M1, of course, also has a dirty postwar history. As a rifle mass-produced to win a world war, the US government has used its vast surplus to arm everyone from the doomed Army of the Republic of Vietnam to modern Haitian cops.

That’s the problem with choosing to honor a firearm in the first place. Killing machines are inherently problematic things. Like most elections, the choice for voters came down to selecting the least worst option, and as they often do, Idaho voters picked the worst one: the Winchester 1873.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
